docs.title: node2vec-rs
docs.text:
node2vec and metapath2vec graph embeddings. The Rust crate does the work: random walks in parallel, then skip-gram with negative sampling trained by lock-free Hogwild! SGD on the CPU. This package is a thin layer over it. Hand in an edge list, get vectors back.

uv pip install node2vec-rs

import node2vec_rs

src = ["a", "a", "b", "c", "c"]
dst = ["b", "c", "c", "d", "e"]

emb = node2vec_rs.node2vec(src, dst, dim=16, walk_length=20)
emb.vectors  # (5, 16) float32
emb.ids  # array(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'])

Typed graph, knowledge graph style? Use metapath2vec:

emb = node2vec_rs.metapath2vec(
    src=["g1", "g2", "g3"],
    dst=["p1", "p1", "p2"],
    node_ids=["g1", "g2", "g3", "p1", "p2"],
    node_types=["gene", "gene", "gene", "pathway", "pathway"],
    metapath="gene-pathway-gene",
)
emb.vectors, emb.ids, emb.types, emb.walk_stats

docs.title: Two functions, no classes
docs.text:
There is nothing to fit and keep: no transform on unseen nodes, no index to query. So node2vec() and metapath2vec() are plain functions returning an Embedding, a frozen dataclass of the vectors and the ids naming each row.

Ids can be strings or integers, and they come back in the dtype they went in as. Edges go in as two equal-length arrays plus an optional weight array, so a polars frame, a networkx graph or a CSV are one line away:

# polars
emb = node2vec_rs.node2vec(df["from"], df["to"], df["weight"])

# networkx
src, dst = zip(*G.edges())
emb = node2vec_rs.node2vec(src, dst)

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
node2vec covers p, q, memory and reproducibility. metapath2vec covers schemas, metapath2vec++ and the walk statistics. The API reference has every argument.

This package versions separately from the Rust crate. Python 0.1.0 wraps node2vec-rs 0.5.0.

docs.title: node2vec
docs.text:
node2vec(
    src: Ids,
    dst: Ids,
    weight: Weights | None = None,
    *,
    directed: bool = False,
    p: float = 1.0,
    q: float = 1.0,
    dim: int = 128,
    walks_per_node: int = 10,
    walk_length: int = 80,
    window: int = 10,
    epochs: int = 5,
    neg: int = 5,
    lr: float = 0.025,
    sample: float = 0.001,
    normalise: bool = True,
    seed: int = 42,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
    verbose: bool = False,
) -> Embedding

Embed the nodes of a homogeneous graph with node2vec.

Second-order biased random walks feed a skip-gram model with negative sampling, trained with lock-free (Hogwild!) SGD.

Memory is dominated by the transition table, keyed on (previous, current) node pairs, so it grows with the sum of squared degrees. Hub-heavy graphs get expensive fast; metapath2vec walks are first-order and do not have this problem.

With more than one thread the threads race on the shared weights, so the vectors differ between runs at the same seed. Pass n_threads=1 for bit-identical output. Walk generation is reproducible at any thread count.

Return parameter. Low values keep the walk local.

1.0 q float

In-out parameter. Low values push the walk outwards (DFS-like), high values keep it near the start (BFS-like).

1.0 dim int

Embedding dimension.

Walks started from every node.

10 walk_length int

Nodes per walk.

Maximum skip-gram context window.

Initial learning rate, decayed linearly towards zero.

Subsampling threshold for frequent nodes. 0 disables it.

docs.text:
metapath2vec(
    src: Ids,
    dst: Ids,
    node_ids: Ids,
    node_types: Ids,
    metapath: str,
    weight: Weights | None = None,
    *,
    plus: bool = False,
    directed: bool = False,
    dim: int = 128,
    walks_per_node: int = 10,
    walk_length: int = 80,
    window: int = 10,
    epochs: int = 5,
    neg: int = 5,
    lr: float = 0.025,
    sample: float = 0.001,
    normalise: bool = True,
    seed: int = 42,
    n_threads: int | None = None,
    verbose: bool = False,
) -> Embedding

Embed the nodes of a heterogeneous graph with metapath2vec.

Walks follow a cyclic schema over node types, e.g. "gene-pathway-gene", and start only on nodes of the schema's first type. The walk is first-order, so memory stays linear in the edge count.

Same reproducibility caveat as node2vec: pass n_threads=1 for bit-identical vectors.

docs.title: Embedding dataclass
docs.text:
Node vectors and the ids that name their rows.

Attributes:

Name Type Description vectors ndarray

(n_nodes, dim) float32 array.

ids ndarray

Node id per row, in the dtype the ids came in as.

types ndarray | None

Node type per row. metapath2vec only.

walk_stats dict[str, int | float] | None

What walk generation produced: start nodes, walks attempted, truncated and dropped, mean realised length and the walk length after rounding up to the schema. metapath2vec only. A high truncated or dropped count means the schema rarely fits the graph and the vectors are not worth much.

docs.title: metapath2vec
docs.text:
metapath2vec is node2vec for typed graphs. The walk follows a schema over node types, say gene-pathway-gene, so a gene only ever steps to a pathway and a pathway only ever steps back to a gene. Two genes end up close when they share pathways, not because some hub happens to sit next to both.

import node2vec_rs

emb = node2vec_rs.metapath2vec(
    src=["g0", "g1", "g2", "g3", "g4", "g5"],
    dst=["pA", "pA", "pA", "pB", "pB", "pB"],
    node_ids=["g0", "g1", "g2", "g3", "g4", "g5", "pA", "pB"],
    node_types=["gene"] * 6 + ["pathway"] * 2,
    metapath="gene-pathway-gene",
    dim=16,
    walk_length=21,
)
emb.walk_stats

docs.title: Nodes and edges
docs.text:
Unlike node2vec(), the nodes come in as their own table: node_ids, unique, and node_types, one type name per id. At most 256 types. Every edge endpoint has to be in node_ids, or you get a ValueError naming the first one that isn't.

Leave weight out and the graph is unweighted, so each step is a single uniform draw over the neighbours of the right type.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
Type names joined by hyphens, closing on the type it started on:

  • gene-pathway-gene
  • author-paper-venue-paper-author
  • drug-target-disease-target-drug

The closing type makes the schema cycle, and walk_length is rounded up to a whole number of cycles. Walks start only on nodes of the first type, so walks_per_node means walks per node of that type. Type names can't contain a hyphen.

A typo in a type name raises Node2VecError with the types the graph does have.

docs.title: metapath2vec++
docs.text: plus=True draws negatives from the context node's own type rather than from every node. A pathway context gets pathway negatives. That is the "++" variant from the paper (Dong, Chawla and Swami, KDD 2017).

docs.title: Check walk_stats
docs.text:
A wrong schema still produces vectors. They're just garbage. walk_stats is the only warning you get:

Key Meaning start_nodes Nodes carrying the schema's first type attempted start_nodes * walks_per_node truncated Walks that hit a dead end before the full length dropped Walks shorter than two nodes, thrown away mean_length Mean length of the surviving walks walk_length Requested length after rounding up to the schema

A high truncated or dropped share means the schema rarely fits the graph. If every walk dead-ends on the first hop, there is nothing to train on and you get a Node2VecError instead.

docs.title: Row order
docs.text:
The rows come back grouped by type, not in node_ids order. emb.ids and emb.types name each row, so index through them:

genes = emb.vectors[emb.types == "gene"]

Nodes no walk ever reaches, a type outside the schema for instance, keep their random initialisation. Filter them out before you use the vectors.

Threads, reproducibility and the training defaults work exactly as in node2vec.

docs.title: node2vec
docs.text:
node2vec runs second-order biased random walks over a homogeneous graph and feeds them to skip-gram. Nodes that turn up in the same walks end up close together.

import itertools

import numpy as np
import node2vec_rs

# Two 8-cliques joined by a single bridge edge.
edges = [
    (f"{side}{i}", f"{side}{j}")
    for side in "ab"
    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(8), 2)
]
edges.append(("a0", "b0"))
src, dst = zip(*edges)

emb = node2vec_rs.node2vec(src, dst, dim=16, walk_length=20, n_threads=1)

side = np.array([i[0] for i in emb.ids])
sim = emb.vectors @ emb.vectors.T  # cosine, rows are unit length
sim[side[:, None] == side[None, :]].mean(), sim[side[:, None] != side[None, :]].mean()

docs.title: The graph
docs.text: src and dst name the endpoints of each edge, weight is optional and must be positive. Undirected by default, so every edge goes in both ways; pass directed=True to keep them one-way. Every node that appears in an edge gets a row in the output, sorted by id. Isolated nodes have no edges to appear in, so they get no row.

docs.title: p and q
docs.text:
The walk is biased by where it just came from.

Low High p (return) Walk keeps doubling back, stays local Walk rarely returns q (in-out) Walk heads outwards, DFS-like, picks up communities Walk hugs the start, BFS-like, picks up structural roles

p = q = 1 is a plain weighted random walk, i.e. DeepWalk.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: The second-order transition table is keyed on (previous, current) node pairs, so it grows with the sum of squared degrees. A few hubs with tens of thousands of neighbours each get painful fast. If that bites, metapath2vec walks are first-order and stay linear in the edge count.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text: dim=128, walks_per_node=10, walk_length=80 and window=10 follow the node2vec paper. lr=0.025, neg=5 and sample=1e-3 are the word2vec defaults. epochs=5. Output rows are L2-normalised unless you pass normalise=False.

docs.title: Threads and reproducibility
docs.text:
All cores by default; n_threads caps it for that call. Hogwild! SGD means the threads write to the shared weight matrices without locks, which is the whole reason it is fast. The flip side: with more than one thread the result changes from run to run at the same seed.

Need bit-identical vectors? Pass n_threads=1. Walk generation itself is reproducible at any thread count.

verbose=True prints how long the graph and the walks took, then one line per epoch:

Built graph with 16 nodes and 56 edges in 0.00s
Generated 160 walks in 0.00s
Training on 160 random walks (12_800 tokens per epoch, 38_400 total)
  Epoch 1/3
  Epoch 2/3
  Epoch 3/3

Training complete in 0.00s (11679425 tokens/sec)

In a terminal the walks and the training get live progress bars on top.
